entities.summary:
Alexander de Brus, Dean of Glasgow, was a younger brother of King Robert I of Scotland, who supported his brother in the struggle for the crown of Scotland.

As a member of the powerful de Brus family, Alexander played a crucial role in the governance of Scotland during the late 13th century. His involvement in the royal succession crisis of 1292-1297 led to his appointment as Dean of Glasgow, a position that gave him significant influence over the church and state in Scotland.

Alexander's legacy extends beyond his own lifetime, as the struggles of the Scottish monarchy in the late 13th century had far-reaching consequences for the development of Scotland and the wider British Isles.

One striking aspect of Alexander's story is the way in which the complexities of Scottish royal politics were shaped by the intersecting forces of family, church, and state. This was a period of great upheaval, as the de Brus family's own claims to the throne were constantly contested by rival claimants and rival powers.

In the end, it was the de Brus family's own internal divisions that ultimately led to the triumph of the rival house of Stewart, and the establishment of a new dynasty that would shape Scotland for centuries to come.

As a historical figure, Alexander de Brus remains an important but relatively overlooked presence in the annals of Scottish history. His story offers a fascinating glimpse into the inner workings of medieval royal politics, and the complex web of alliances and rivalries that shaped the fate of the Scottish monarchy.
